allowed_dependency_manifest.content: Let n, k, l ∈ Z with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n. Define R(q) = [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q in the natural rational-function setting for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients. If R(q) lies in a polynomial ring in q (i.e., R(q) has only finitely many nonnegative powers of q with coefficients in the relevant coefficient ring), then when written as R(q) = Σ_i c_i q^i, every coefficient c_i satisfies c_i ≥ 0.

forbidden_claims.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

payload.previous_proof_nl:
Let K be an algebraic closure of k, and set J := I K[x_1,...,x_d] inside K[x_1,...,x_d]. The weighted grading and the homogeneity of I are not needed for the argument.

First handle the case d = 0. Then S = k. The affine 0-space over K has exactly one point, namely the origin. If I = S, then its zero locus is empty, contrary to the hypothesis that the zero locus is exactly the origin. Hence I = 0, so S/I is isomorphic to k, which is finite-dimensional over k.

Now assume d >= 1. The common zero locus of J in K^d is the same as the common zero locus of I in K^d: every element of I lies in J, and every element of J is a finite K[x_1,...,x_d]-linear combination of elements of I, so a point of K^d annihilates all elements of I if and only if it annihilates all elements of J. By hypothesis, V(J) = {0}.

Because K is algebraically closed, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz gives that the radical of J is the ideal of all polynomials vanishing on V(J). Since V(J) = {0}, this ideal is exactly (x_1,...,x_d). Therefore, for each i = 1,...,d, we have x_i in rad(J), so there exists an integer N_i >= 1 such that x_i^(N_i) belongs to J.

We next prove that J intersect S = I. The inclusion I subseteq J intersect S is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, let f be an element of J intersect S. Since f belongs to J, there exist finitely many elements g_1,...,g_m of I and polynomials A_1,...,A_m in K[x_1,...,x_d] such that
f = sum_{r=1}^m A_r g_r.
Let V be the finite-dimensional k-subspace of K spanned by 1 and by all coefficients of all the A_r. Choose a k-basis b_1,...,b_t of V with b_1 = 1. Since every coefficient of each A_r lies in V, we can write uniquely
A_r = sum_{s=1}^t b_s B_{r,s}
with B_{r,s} in S = k[x_1,...,x_d]. Hence
f = sum_{s=1}^t b_s G_s,
where G_s := sum_{r=1}^m B_{r,s} g_r belongs to I for each s.
Now set H_1 := G_1 - f and H_s := G_s for s > 1. Then each H_s lies in S, and
sum_{s=1}^t b_s H_s = 0
in K[x_1,...,x_d]. Write each H_s as a finite sum
H_s = sum_alpha c_{s,alpha} x^alpha
with c_{s,alpha} in k. Since the monomials x^alpha are linearly independent over K in the polynomial ring K[x_1,...,x_d], for each multi-index alpha we get
sum_{s=1}^t b_s c_{s,alpha} = 0
in K. But b_1,...,b_t are k-linearly independent, and each c_{s,alpha} lies in k. Therefore all c_{s,alpha} are zero. So every H_s is the zero polynomial. In particular H_1 = 0, hence f = G_1 belongs to I. This proves J intersect S = I.

Applying this to x_i^(N_i), we obtain x_i^(N_i) in I for every i. Therefore any monomial x_1^(a_1) ... x_d^(a_d) with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, because it is divisible by x_i^(N_i). It follows that the residue classes of the finitely many monomials x_1^(a_1) ... x_d^(a_d) with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i span S/I over k. Hence S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

Thus the lemma is proved.

result_payload.addressed_previous_feedback: Yes. I removed the Nullstellensatz/radical step entirely and replaced it by a localization-at-x_i argument plus a self-contained proof of Zariski's lemma. I kept the explicit proof that J intersect S = I and the bounded-monomial spanning argument.
result_payload.proof_nl:
Let K be an algebraic closure of k, and let J := I K[x_1,...,x_d] inside K[x_1,...,x_d]. The grading hypotheses are not needed in the argument below.

First note that I and J have the same common zeroes in K^d. Indeed, I is contained in J, so every zero of J is a zero of I. Conversely, if a in K^d satisfies f(a)=0 for every f in I, then for any g in J we can write g as a finite sum g = sum_r A_r f_r with A_r in K[x_1,...,x_d] and f_r in I, hence g(a) = sum_r A_r(a) f_r(a) = 0. Therefore the common zero locus of J in K^d is also exactly the origin.

First handle the case d = 0. Then S = k. The affine 0-space over K has exactly one point, namely the origin. If I = S, its zero locus is empty, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence I = 0, so S/I = k, which is finite-dimensional over k.

Now assume d >= 1.

We first prove that for each i = 1,...,d, some power of x_i lies in J.

Set R := K[x_1,...,x_d]/J, and let x_i also denote its image in R. Suppose for contradiction that x_i is not nilpotent in R. Then the localization R_{x_i} is nonzero: if R_{x_i} were zero, then 1/1 = 0 in R_{x_i}, so by the definition of localization there would exist N >= 0 with x_i^N = 0 in R, contradicting the assumption that x_i is not nilpotent.

Choose a maximal ideal m of the nonzero ring R_{x_i}, and let L := R_{x_i}/m. Then L is a field. Also L is a finitely generated K-algebra, because R_{x_i} is isomorphic to K[x_1,...,x_d,u]/(J,ux_i-1), hence is generated over K by the images of x_1,...,x_d and u.

We now prove the needed field-theoretic fact.

Sublemma (Zariski's lemma). If a field L is finitely generated as a K-algebra, then L is algebraic over K.

Proof of sublemma. Write L = K[alpha_1,...,alpha_n]. Let alpha_1,...,alpha_r be a transcendence basis of L over K. Put R0 := K[alpha_1,...,alpha_r]. For each j > r, the element alpha_j is algebraic over K(alpha_1,...,alpha_r), so there exists a nonzero polynomial equation
c_j alpha_j^{m_j} + a_{j,m_j-1} alpha_j^{m_j-1} + ... + a_{j,0} = 0
with c_j, a_{j,l} in R0 and c_j != 0. Let f be the product of the finitely many c_j (with the empty product equal to 1 if r = n), and set B := R0[1/f]. Since 1/c_j belongs to B for every j > r, each displayed equation can be divided by c_j, so each alpha_j for j > r is integral over B. Hence L = B[alpha_{r+1},...,alpha_n] is integral over B.

If a field is integral over a subring, then that subring is itself a field: indeed, let 0 != b in B. Since b^{-1} belongs to the field L and L is integral over B, the element b^{-1} satisfies a monic equation
(b^{-1})^m + b_{m-1}(b^{-1})^{m-1} + ... + b_0 = 0
with b_t in B. Multiplying by b^{m-1} gives
b^{-1} = -(b_{m-1} + b_{m-2}b + ... + b_0 b^{m-1}),
so b^{-1} belongs to B. Therefore B is a field.

We claim this is impossible if r >= 1. Indeed, consider g := f alpha_1 + 1 in R0. If g were invertible in B = R0[1/f], then for some h in R0 and some N >= 0 we would have g h = f^N in R0. But 1 = g - alpha_1 f, so the ideals (g,f) and R0 coincide. Hence in the quotient ring R0/(g), the image of f is a unit, and therefore the image of f^N is also a unit. On the other hand, g h = f^N implies f^N = 0 in R0/(g). This is impossible because R0/(g) is nonzero: g has positive degree in alpha_1, so it is not a unit of the polynomial ring R0. Thus g is not invertible in B, so B is not a field. Contradiction.

Therefore r = 0. So L is algebraic over K. This proves the sublemma.

Applying the sublemma to our field L, we conclude that L is algebraic over K. Since K is algebraically closed, L = K.

Let a_j be the image of x_j in L = K. Every element of J maps to 0 in R and hence to 0 in L, so f(a_1,...,a_d)=0 for all f in J. But x_i is invertible in R_{x_i}, hence its image a_i in L is nonzero. Therefore (a_1,...,a_d) is a nonzero common zero of J in K^d, contradicting that the common zero locus of J is exactly the origin. This contradiction shows that x_i is nilpotent in R. So there exists N_i >= 1 such that x_i^{N_i} belongs to J.

Next we prove that J intersect S = I.

The inclusion I subseteq J intersect S is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, let f be an element of J intersect S. Since f belongs to J, there exist finitely many elements g_1,...,g_m of I and polynomials A_1,...,A_m in K[x_1,...,x_d] such that
f = sum_{r=1}^m A_r g_r.
Let V be the finite-dimensional k-subspace of K spanned by 1 and by all coefficients of all the A_r. Choose a k-basis b_1,...,b_t of V with b_1 = 1. Since every coefficient of each A_r lies in V, we can write uniquely
A_r = sum_{s=1}^t b_s B_{r,s}
with B_{r,s} in S = k[x_1,...,x_d]. Hence
f = sum_{s=1}^t b_s G_s,
where G_s := sum_{r=1}^m B_{r,s} g_r belongs to I for every s.
Now set H_1 := G_1 - f and H_s := G_s for s > 1. Then each H_s lies in S, and
sum_{s=1}^t b_s H_s = 0
in K[x_1,...,x_d]. Write each H_s as a finite sum
H_s = sum_alpha c_{s,alpha} x^alpha
with c_{s,alpha} in k. Since the monomials x^alpha are linearly independent over K in the polynomial ring K[x_1,...,x_d], for each multi-index alpha we get
sum_{s=1}^t b_s c_{s,alpha} = 0
in K. But b_1,...,b_t are k-linearly independent, and each c_{s,alpha} lies in k. Therefore all c_{s,alpha} are zero. So every H_s is the zero polynomial. In particular H_1 = 0, hence f = G_1 belongs to I. This proves J intersect S = I.

Applying this to x_i^{N_i}, we obtain x_i^{N_i} in I for every i. Therefore any monomial x_1^{a_1} ... x_d^{a_d} with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, because it is divisible by x_i^{N_i}. It follows that the residue classes of the finitely many monomials x_1^{a_1} ... x_d^{a_d} with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i span S/I over k. Hence S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

Thus the lemma is proved.
result_payload.proof_summary: After base change to an algebraic closure K, let J = I K[x_1,...,x_d]. The zero loci of I and J in K^d coincide. For each i, if no power of x_i lay in J, then the localization (K[x]/J)_{x_i} would be nonzero. A maximal ideal quotient of this localization is a field finitely generated over K; a self-contained proof of Zariski's lemma shows it must equal K, yielding a nonzero K-point of V(J), contradiction. Hence x_i^{N_i} is in J for every i. An explicit coefficient-separation argument proves J intersect S = I, so x_i^{N_i} is actually in I. Then only finitely many monomials survive modulo I, and these span S/I over k. Therefore S/I is finite-dimensional over k.
